actualProfilesRead.name: Econometrics
actualProfilesRead.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

actualProfilesRead.name: Consumer Product Design
actualProfilesRead.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
actualProfilesRead.profile: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.

actualProfilesRead.name: Research Methods & Statistics
actualProfilesRead.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.

actualProfilesRead.name: Personal Leadership
actualProfilesRead.description2: Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead confidently in any setting.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Personal Leadership is an interactive course for Liberal Arts and Sciences students that introduces leadership fundamentals with a focus on self-awareness and practical skills. Through a blend of theory, interaction, and assessments, students will cultivate the tools needed to lead effectively in both personal and professional contexts. The course begins by exploring leadership fundamentals, emphasizing transformational leadership (Bass, 1990) and authentic leadership (Gardner et al., 2021), supported by foundational concepts from Northouse’s Leadership: Theory and Practice (2025), which offers a balanced overview of various leadership models and their applications. Covey’s (2020) The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: 30th Anniversary Edition provides a foundation for principles such as proactive behavior, prioritization, and fostering collaboration. Students critically analyze these concepts through evolutionary perspectives on adaptive strategies (Lonati & Van Vugt, 2023) and apply Locke and Latham’s (2019) goal-setting theory to develop actionable leadership plans. Self-awareness and emotional intelligence (Goleman, 2021) are central themes, with students engaging in reflective exercises, group discussions, and personality assessments to better understand their strengths, values, and leadership styles. The course maximizes interaction through workshops, group projects, role-playing, and peer feedback sessions, ensuring active engagement and collaboration.
actualProfilesRead.topics: proactive behavior; fostering collaboration; unique leadership style; personal leadership; core leadership principles; lead confidently

actualProfilesRead.name: Leadership Communication
actualProfilesRead.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Communication and leadership are two sides of the same coin; Quintilian, the famous Roman Professor of Rhetoric, knew this when he famously declared that the best leader is ‘the good person speaking well’. At the start of this course, the participants will be introduced the main leadership and communication models and theories. They will also read leading articles from the Harvard Business Review on leadership communication. Theories that will be explored will include transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership approaches. We will also explore the roles of gender, ethics and culture in communicative leadership positions. The module will focus on the role of emotional intelligence in communicating leadership; touching on key matters such as empathy, ethics, self-awareness and self-regulation. The course will also have a distinctive liberal arts and sciences flavour to it, analysing the leadership qualities and deficiencies of characters in prose fiction, film and drama. It is especially in the worlds created by Shakespeare, where key lessons about how to lead, and how not to lead, can be learned by the leaders of tomorrow. The course will also bring in real leaders from outside the college, from both the business and public sectors, to interact with the students on the subject matter of their own communicative leadership experiences and goals. Such interactions with entrepreneurial and industry heads may lead to spin-off internships in the following academic year.

Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. actualProfilesRead.profile: People are the organisation. Without people, organisations cannot survive or be productive. This course, tailored for Liberal Arts and Sciences bachelor students, offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the psychological, social, and structural dynamics within organisations. It equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence organisational environments effectively throughout their academic and professional careers. Drawing on foundational and contemporary research in organisational behaviour, this upper- level undergraduate course incorporates a case-based approach that includes conceptual frameworks, case discussions, and skill-building activities. Students will explore topics such as motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and organizational culture using Robbins and Judge’s (2023) Organisational Behaviour as a primary resource. Additional literature and materials will supplement the course to provide a well-rounded perspective. Topics Covered => Core Concepts: Diversity in organisations, attitudes and job satisfaction, emotions and moods, personality and values, perception and decision-making, motivation, communication, leadership, power and politics, and conflict and negotiation. Structural Dynamics: The structure and culture of organisations, group behaviour, work teams, and organisational change. These topics are structured within a comprehensive model that defines the field of organisational behaviour and outlines its key concepts and relationships.

actualProfilesRead.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
actualProfilesRead.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
actualProfilesRead.profile: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence; whether in business, leadership, or life. The course offers an immersive, practice-driven exploration of negotiation as both an analytical discipline and a strategic interpersonal skill. Students will engage in frequent simulations, role-plays, and reflective exercises designed to build confidence and adaptability into the dynamics that shape successful agreements. The course introduces the foundational theories and frameworks that define modern negotiation practice, including BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement), ZOPA analysis (zone of possible agreement), interest-based negotiation, and the dual-concern model. There will also be a focus on (i) avoiding bargaining over positions, (ii) separating people from the problem, (iii) focusing on interests not positions, (iv) inventing options for mutual gain, and (v) insisting on using objective criteria. Students will learn to diagnose negotiation structures, identify value-creation opportunities, and strategically manage trade-offs (e.g. logrolling). Core concepts such as anchoring, framing, concession patterns, and the psychology of influence will be woven throughout weekly activities. Because negotiation is inseparable from human behavior, the course integrates research from social psychology and language & communication studies.
actualProfilesRead.topics: batna (best alternative to a negotiated agreement); zopa analysis (zone of possible agreement); interest-based negotiation; dual-concern model; concession patterns; craft persuasive arguments

actualProfilesRead.name: AI Ethics
actualProfilesRead.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.

actualProfilesRead.name: Linear Algebra
actualProfilesRead.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.

actualProfilesRead.name: Governance of Sustainability
actualProfilesRead.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
actualProfilesRead.profile: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.

actualProfilesRead.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
actualProfilesRead.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
actualProfilesRead.profile: The production of food is a contentious topic in our modern society. Current farming methods are major contributors to environmental harm worldwide. However, the human population is expected to continue to grow to 10 billion before peaking, with the greatest growth forecast in developing countries. Sustainable farming is the approach where both food needs and environmental impact are balanced. As current farming practices are generally more concerned about output than impact, change is necessary to ensure a sustainable future, while still ensuring the human population can be fed adequately. In this course we will learn about and discuss different aspects of farming that contribute to future plans and directions of sustainable farming on a global scale. Current practices and environmental impacts will be presented, to understand where we are starting from. Current alternatives will be critically assessed, to understand how we might progress. Innovations and modern approaches will be researched, to understand where we might end up. The purpose of this course is not to convince you of what the right way forward is, but to present information objectively, so that you can make up your own mind and help build a more sustainable future.
actualProfilesRead.topics: sustainable livestock farming; integrated pest management; sustainable supply chains; organic farming; crop rotation; precision agriculture

actualProfilesRead.name: Sustainability Essentials I
actualProfilesRead.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
actualProfilesRead.profile: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3

actualProfilesRead.name: Climate Change
actualProfilesRead.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
actualProfilesRead.topics: renewable energy systems; carbon dioxide storage; climate-adaptive spatial planning; anthropogenic climate change; ocean acidification; carbon storage

actualProfilesRead.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
actualProfilesRead.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
actualProfilesRead.profile: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3

actualProfilesRead.name: Ethics
actualProfilesRead.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
actualProfilesRead.topics: animal rights; future generations; climate change; historical injustice; moral reasoning virtue; reasoning virtue ethics

actualProfilesRead.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
actualProfilesRead.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
actualProfilesRead.topics: qualitative research methodology; conducting small team; interpreting meaning; power dynamics; reflecting; covers designing

actualProfilesRead.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
actualProfilesRead.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
actualProfilesRead.profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way.
